facts.text: Carmen premiered at the Opéra-Comique in Paris on 3 March 1875, and its broken conventions shocked its first audiences.
facts.evidence: The opera was first performed by the Opéra-Comique in Paris on 3 March 1875, where its breaking of conventions shocked and scandalised its first audiences.

facts.text: Bizet died suddenly of heart disease the day after the 33rd performance, at 36. He never knew Carmen would conquer the world.
evidence: the day after the opera's 33rd performance, Bizet died suddenly of heart disease, at the age of 36
unaware that the work would achieve international acclaim

facts.text: The Habanera is based on “El arreglito” by Sebastián Yradier. Bizet thought it was a folk tune; when he found out, he credited Yradier in the score.
evidence: Carmen's habanera is based on an idiomatic song, "El arreglito", by the Spanish composer Sebastián Yradier
when he learned its recent origin he added a note to the vocal score, crediting Yradier

facts.text: Bizet also rewrote the words of Carmen’s Habanera himself.
facts.evidence: he provided new words for Carmen's "Habanera"

facts.text: Bizet was reportedly contemptuous of the Toreador Song: “Well, they asked for ordure, and they’ve got it.”
facts.evidence: Well, they asked for ordure, and they've got it

facts.text: Micaëla brings Don José a letter and a kiss from his mother. The librettists added her to soften the story for the family theatre.
evidence: Micaëla returns and gives José a letter and a kiss from his mother
offset by Micaëla, described by Halévy as "a very innocent, very chaste young girl"

facts.text: The Opéra-Comique’s co-director, de Leuven, opposed staging such a risqué story in what he considered a family theatre.
facts.evidence: De Leuven had vociferously opposed the entire notion of presenting so risqué a story in what he considered a family theatre

facts.text: At the premiere, the only applause in Act III was for Micaëla’s aria, as the audience grew more and more uneasy.
facts.evidence: In act 3 only Micaëla's aria earned applause as the audience became increasingly disconcerted.

facts.text: The next day’s reviews ranged from disappointment to outrage. One critic called Galli-Marié’s Carmen “the very incarnation of vice”.
evidence: The general tone of the next day's press reviews ranged from disappointment to outrage.

facts.text: After the premiere Bizet reportedly said: “Don’t you see that all these bourgeois have not understood a wretched word of the work I have written for them?”
facts.attribution: Bizet, as reported by Benjamin Godard (via Wikipedia)
facts.evidence: Don't you see that all these bourgeois have not understood a wretched word of the work I have written for them?

facts.text: Tchaikovsky wrote to his patron Nadezhda von Meck: “Carmen is a masterpiece in every sense of the word.”
facts.attribution: Tchaikovsky, letter to Nadezhda von Meck (via Wikipedia)
facts.evidence: Carmen is a masterpiece in every sense of the word

facts.text: Brahms reportedly saw Carmen twenty times and said he would have “gone to the ends of the earth to embrace Bizet”.
evidence: It also won praise from both Wagner and Brahms.
The latter reportedly saw the opera twenty times, and said he would have "gone to the ends of the earth to embrace Bizet".

facts.text: Carmen first played at the Metropolitan Opera on 9 January 1884, to mixed reviews.
facts.evidence: On 9 January 1884, Carmen was given its first New York Metropolitan Opera performance, to a mixed critical reception.

facts.text: Enrico Caruso sang José on the Met tour in San Francisco on 17 April 1906. Two hours later the great earthquake hit, and the singers fled the Palace Hotel.
evidence: On 17 April 1906, on tour with the Met, he sang the role at the Grand Opera House in San Francisco.
Two hours later he was awakened by the first violent shocks of the 1906 San Francisco earthquake

facts.text: Bizet was still revising Carmen when he died, and later changes (like Guiraud’s recitatives) mean there is still no definitive edition.
facts.evidence: there is still no definitive edition of the opera

facts.text: Before the last scene, a chorus and procession announce the toreador Escamillo: “Vivat, vivat le Toréro!”
facts.evidence: a chorus and procession announces the arrival of the toreador Escamillo
